result: The authors generated a panel of 182 recombinant inbred advanced intercross lines (RIAILs) from N2 and CB4856 strains and performed high-throughput imaging of ~12 million microscopy pictures from 9,641 embryos. They observed extensive quantitative variations in spindle characteristics across the RIAIL panel with statistically significant broad-sense heritability for all spindle traits.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this as a 'tour de force' imaging effort and did not question the RIAIL generation or the observation of extensive variations. The acceptance summary explicitly praises 'imaging 182 lines of C. elegans embryos during the first division to infer their scaling and positioning,' indicating reviewer acceptance of these foundational experimental claims.

result: The authors tested different models for spindle length regulation using correlation analyses across RIAILs. They found that final spindle length is highly correlated with cell length (p = 7.96E-55) but not with initial spindle length (p = 0.17) or cell volume when conditioned on cell length (p = 0.13), ruling out Timer and simple Limiting Component models. They also found positive correlation with centrosome distance, ruling out the simplest Boundary model.
evaluation: While reviewers did not directly challenge the correlation data, they requested clarification on 'the link between partial correlations and correlations' (Round 2, comment 4), stating 'this does not seem to be obvious.' This indicates the reviewers found the statistical reasoning and interpretation of these correlations insufficiently explained, creating uncertainty about the strength of the conclusions drawn from these analyses.

result: Through conditional QTL mapping, the authors identified two QTLs on chromosome III (QTL1 and QTL2) that explain 21% and 10% of variation in final spindle length independent of cell length, respectively. QTL1 overlapped with gpr-1 and QTL2 with par-2. RNAi knockdowns of both genes resulted in shorter final spindle length, with the authors claiming PAR-2 regulates final spindle length in addition to its known role in positioning.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated 'The fact that gpr-1/2 and par-2 are important regulators of spindle elongation during anaphase, and thus of final spindle length has been demonstrated many years ago. Therefore I'm not convinced that the QTL analysis performed in this study really highlights a novel feature' (Round 1, comment 6). This indicates reviewers viewed these findings as confirmatory rather than novel, questioning whether the QTL analysis added significant new understanding beyond existing knowledge.

result: Through laser ablation experiments (cup-cuts parallel and perpendicular to spindle axis, plane-cuts through spindle) and genetic perturbations (spd-1 RNAi), the authors concluded that astral MTs are subject to net pulling forces in multiple directions, that spindle elasticity and central spindle forces have minimal impact on final centrosome position, and that final spindle length is determined by a balance of pulling forces acting in different directions on centrosomes.
evaluation: Reviewers raised substantial concerns about these conclusions. They noted potential 'intrinsic caveats' in laser ablation experiments and stated 'important controls are missing to draw strong conclusions (e.g. genetic evidence to back up their laser-ablation experiments and immunofluorescent staining of microtubules following ablation)' (Round 1, comment 1). More critically, reviewers identified a 'clear discrepancy between the stoichiometric model proposed here and previously published work' by Garzon-Coral et al., 2016, which found pushing forces during anaphase (Round 2, comment 1). Reviewers also noted that 'all the ablation experiments...have been performed on the posterior half of the spindle' and requested anterior controls (Round 1, comment 2).

result: The authors developed a Stoichiometric Model where each cortical force generator (CFG) can bind only one microtubule at a time, with forces along MT directions. Simulations showed that centrosomes stably position at finite distances from cell boundaries regardless of starting position or CFG number. The stoichiometric interaction prevents destabilizing feedback present in models without this constraint, allowing cortical pulling forces alone to stably position centrosomes.
evaluation: Reviewers expressed significant concerns about the model explanation and parameters. They stated 'The authors did not do a good job in explaining the mechanism by which the stoichiometric model leads to centrosome centering' and urged authors 'to explain the mechanism of stabilizing the central centrosome position and not just to state that their mechanism does so' (Round 1, comment 9). Regarding parameters, reviewers noted the catastrophe rate used (0.025/s) 'seems extremely low' and they 'could not find this number anywhere' in the cited manuscript, while 'Kozlowski et al. used a cortical catastrophe rate in anaphase of 1 to 10/s' (Round 2, comment 3). Reviewers also noted lack of detail about the stochastic simulation implementation (Round 1, comment 8).

result: The Stoichiometric Model predicts that two centrosomes compete for CFGs, and removing one centrosome allows the remaining one to move to the cell center. Laser ablation experiments confirmed this prediction, with the remaining centrosome consistently centering in 13 embryos, supporting that one centrosome modulates forces on the other.
evaluation: While reviewers did not directly challenge this specific experiment, they noted a critical discrepancy with prior work: 'the single centrosome experiment performed in (Krueger et al., 2010) (through zyg-1(RNAi)...is in disagreement with results presented here (where a single centrosome, obtained after laser ablation of the other centrosome during metaphase, moved to the cell center)' (Round 2, comment 2). In Krueger et al., the single centrosome came to rest at 60% egg length, not at the center, creating uncertainty about the interpretation and generalizability of the single centrosome centering result.

result: The Stoichiometric Model with asymmetric CFG distribution (50% more posterior than anterior) quantitatively reproduces spindle elongation dynamics, positioning, and scaling relationships with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species spanning 100 million years of evolution. The model explains variations in final spindle length, centrosome distance from cortex, spindle center position, and elongation rate across all datasets tested.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the model 'explains the dynamics and variability of spindle scaling' in the acceptance summary, they raised concerns about whether it 'represents a significant advance' over the Bouvrais et al., 2018 model, which 'fully accounts for the effect of the LET-99 loss-of-function observed in vivo' (Round 1, comment 5). Critically, reviewers noted 'the role of LET-99 is completely ignored in the stoichiometric model' and emphasized that Krueger et al., 2010 showed 'LET-99 inhibits lateral posterior pulling forces,' which is inconsistent with the model's assumption of uniform posterior pulling forces (Round 2, comment 2). This omission creates uncertainty about whether the model captures the full biological complexity.
